astra.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think it's a little bit of both. So the interesting idea is that you don't necessarily need paired data between every pair of modalities, right? If you have different modalities paired with images, then images can serve as a common reference. By learning to align with that reference, these modalities can also become aligned with each other, even without directly observing those pairs during training. I think that's the more general idea, and it's not necessarily specific to images.

But why images? I think that does have a lot to do with the data. Images contain very rich information about the world, and it's natural to have other information associated with them. So it's a very convenient place to make these connections. And that connects to our earlier discussion, right? What data is available really influences what kind of system we can build.

But I wouldn't say that vision is necessarily the best hub for everything. If some information in another modality isn't reflected in the image, then aligning through images may not be enough to learn that information. So sharing an embedding space doesn't mean you've captured every aspect of every modality.

So, yeah, I would separate the general idea of learning connections through a shared modality from the particular choice of vision. The first is quite general, I think. The second depends a lot on the data and on what you want the model to do.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think it is a little bit of both. There is a deeper reason that vision can serve as a hub, because many modalities describe the same physical event. An image of a scene is naturally related to its audio, its depth, its thermal signal, or the motion of the camera. So if each modality is aligned with vision, they can become aligned with one another even without direct paired data between every pair of modalities. That was the surprising result in ImageBind.

But I would not claim that vision is uniquely the universal hub. It is also a contingent fact that we have a lot of image-paired data at internet scale, especially image-text and image-audio data, and strong pretrained image encoders. If another modality had equally broad coverage and sufficiently rich paired data, perhaps it could play the same role. So the deeper statement, for me, is less that image must be the hub and more that you do not need all pairwise combinations. A shared anchor modality can bind many modalities into one representation space, and vision happens to be a particularly natural and practical anchor for the data we have today.

Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's a, that's a great question. so I, I would say honestly it's, it's mostly the second one, the contingent fact. and, and the, the reason is very practical. if you look at how these paired datasets come to exist, images or, or video frames, they are the thing that co-occurs with everything else, right? audio comes with video, so you, you naturally get image-audio pairs. depth comes from RGB-D sensors, where the, the depth camera is literally sitting next to the, the RGB camera. thermal, same thing. IMU comes from, from, egocentric video where the headset is recording motion and, and frames at the same time. So the image is the hub, not because there's something, like, ontologically special about vision, but because the camera happens to be physically bolted next to every other sensor we have. It's, it's kind of a, an accident of how sensors are built and how data gets collected on the internet.

but, but I, I do think there's a, a slightly deeper part, which is the emergent alignment. that was the, the surprising result for us, that if you bind audio to image and you bind depth to image, you, you get audio-to-depth for free, without ever seeing a single audio-depth pair. So the, the hub structure does propagate, and that, that does say something, I, I think, about the, the geometry of these representation spaces. but even that, I, I would frame it as, as a statement about, like, if you have a, a sufficiently dense hub with, with enough coverage, then, then transitivity kind of works out. It doesn't have to be images. and, and in fact, you can see this now, right? in most modern multimodal systems, the hub has kind of shifted to text, to, to the LLM token space, because language is what you want to, to output at the end, and language has, has pairings with almost everything too, just, just through captions and, and descriptions.

So my, my take is the hub is whatever modality your data collection process happens to center on. images were the answer in 2023 because that's, that's where the pairs were. and, and if tomorrow everybody's wearing, you know, glasses that record audio plus IMU plus, plus whatever, the, the hub might, might move again. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah. Right. So ImageBind, the setup is, we have several modalities—image, text, audio, depth, thermal, IMU—and we want them all to live in the same embedding space. But we don’t have paired data between every pair. We don’t have audio paired with depth, or IMU paired with text. What we do have is each of those modalities paired with images. So we use the image as this binding modality, this hub, and we train only with those image pairs. And it turns out the other modalities also align with each other, even though they never saw each other during training. That’s the interesting part.

On your question, I think it’s more the second. I wouldn’t claim it’s a deep statement that vision is inherently a hub modality in some theoretical sense. Vision is a very rich modality, that’s true. It carries a lot of semantic information that overlaps with audio, with language, with 3D. You see a dog, you can imagine the bark, you can imagine the shape. So there is a reason it can serve as this common ground.

But a large part of why it works is contingent on data. Images are just where the paired data exists at scale. That’s how internet data is collected. People take photos, they write captions, videos come with audio, some sensors give you depth with RGB. Images happen to be the most connected node in this pairing graph. If we had audio paired with everything at the same scale, maybe audio could play that role. We didn’t really test that, because the data isn’t there.

So this is consistent with what I was saying earlier. Data availability, how the data is structured, often determines more than some inherent property of the modality itself. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting question. I think it's probably a bit of both, but I would lean towards vision naturally serving as a bridge because of how we interact with the physical world and how data is collected. 

If you think about it, vision is almost always the common denominator across different sensors and recordings. When you record video, you naturally get audio paired with visual frames. When you have autonomous driving setups or robotics, you have depth sensors or LiDAR paired with RGB cameras. Thermal cameras or IMU sensors are also typically mounted alongside visual cameras. So practically, in terms of data availability and the way we build recording devices, vision is naturally co-occurring with almost everything.

And conceptually, vision has that rich spatial grounding that something like text doesn't completely have for low-level signals. People often think of text as a hub modality—and text is great for bridging high-level semantic concepts—but text doesn't naturally pair with raw depth or raw audio or IMU data in the same direct, continuous physical way that an image does. 

So because vision is paired with all these other modalities naturally, it allows us to bypass the need for all-to-all paired data. You don't need to find a dataset that pairs thermal data directly with audio, which is very rare. You can just bind each of them to images, and the joint embedding space emerges naturally through that hub. So yeah, I think it's partly how rich visual information is, but very much also a practical reflection of how multimodal data naturally exists in the physical world.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's, that's a great question. I, I would say, honestly, I lean more towards, the, the contingent side, I think. it's, it's mostly a practical fact about, about data availability. So if you think about it, at that time, and still, largely today, images are the, the modality that has, natural pairing with almost everything else, right? You have image-text pairs at billion scale from, from internet, alt-text, captions. You have video, which is, image plus audio, plus, temporal information. Depth, thermal, IMU, these sensors are typically, captured alongside an, an RGB image. But if you want, say, audio-text pairs without, going through images, or depth-audio pairs, it's, it's actually very hard to, to collect those at, at scale. So the choice of image as the, the binding modality was really, driven by where the, the paired data is. It's, it's less of a, a deep, principled, decision and more of, like, this is, this is the only thing we could, we could do if we want to align, everything, without having to, to collect all the, pairwise, combinations, right? That would be, quadratically more expensive.

but, but that, that being said, I, I wouldn't completely rule out, something deeper. I think there is something special about, vision in that, it's, it's a very dense, very information-rich modality about the physical world. Like depth and thermal, these are kind of, different projections, different views of the, the same underlying 3D scene that an image, also captures. So in that sense, image is a, a natural, meeting point for, for these physical, modalities. and also it, it aligns well with, how humans perceive the world, right?

But yeah, overall I, I, I tend to think it's, it's more about the data. And, interestingly, I think the field has, has kind of moved on to, a different hub now. In, in the LLaVA-style models we, we talked about earlier, everything gets encoded into tokens and fed into an LLM, so, language, or the LLM, becomes the, the hub. And that's also for practical reasons, right? We have very strong LLMs, and text is the natural interface for, for users.

So, yeah, I think which modality is the hub is, is less of a, a deep statement and more about, where the data is and, and what the practical usage looks like. Yeah.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's a good question. I would say it's, it's more the second one, honestly. It's, it's largely a, a contingent fact about, about data. So, so the reason we chose image as the, the hub modality, the, the center, is, is very practical. Images are, are the one modality that naturally co-occurs with everything else on, on the internet, right? You have image and text from, from web alt text. You have video, so image and audio come together for free. Depth sensors, they, they always capture an RGB frame alongside the depth. Thermal cameras, same thing. IMU on your phone, on your, egocentric video, there's a camera right there. So we didn't have to, to collect any, any new paired data for, for most of these. It's, it's just what the world gives you.

And, and the second reason is also very practical, is that we already had a very strong image-text embedding space from, from CLIP, from, from OpenCLIP. So if you bind everything to image, you, you get text for free. That's, that's where the, the emergent, alignment comes from, right? We never train audio with text, but audio can retrieve text because they both, live in the, the image space. So, so that, that was, kind of the, the trick.

But, but I would, I would push back a little on, on the idea that it's a, a deep statement that image is, is special. I, I think if you look at what people are doing now, the, the hub has actually moved to, to language, right? To, to the LLM. Everything gets tokenized and, and fed into the, the language model, and, and text is the, the thing that connects all of it. So, so the hub is really just, whichever modality has the most paired data and, and the strongest, pretrained representation at, at the time. In, in 2023, that was, image. Today it's, it's arguably text. And, and maybe in the future, video, because video has, has everything in it, right? It has audio, it has motion, it has, it has temporal, structure.

So, so I think, again, it goes back to, to what I was saying. It's, it's the data. Not, not the, the architecture, not, not even the, the choice of, of which modality is, is in the center. It's, it's where the, the paired data is. Yeah.
